## Overview

The Konjo, also called BaKonzo, Bakonzo, Mukonzo, Bayiira, Banande, or Abanyarwenzururu, are a Bantu ethnic group associated with the Rwenzori region. In Uganda they live in districts including Kasese, Bundibugyo, Bunyangabu and Ntoroko, while Konzo speakers also live on the western slopes of the Rwenzori range in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The 2014 census recorded 850,646 people. Their settlements extend across plains, hills and mountain slopes up to an altitude of 2,200 meters in the Rwenzori Mountains. The sources describe agricultural and animal-husbanding practices, a system of 14 clans and totems, distinctive birth-order names, circumcision and marriage rituals, and historical association with the Rwenzururu movement and kingdom.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

In the marriage account, *Omuseye wa maama* is described historically as a metallic silver or gold wrist band confirming an agreement between families. In the account given for contemporary marriage arrangements, it can include a *gomesi*, shoes, *Ekikoye*, a thick cotton fabric worn underneath, an *Ekitambalha kyo kwamutwe*, a cloth covering the head, a gomesi sash, and money for undergarments or tailoring. The sources also mention bed sheets wrapped in a blanket as part of the *Omukagha*, or dowry.

### Architecture

The sources describe a temporary circumcision structure called *Omupinda*. It was a hut built near or at a river for the annual *Olhusumba* ceremony and dismantled after the ceremony. The river served as a treatment place, where candidates sat in cold water twice a day during healing. In the marriage account, the construction of a new house for a young couple is called *Erityandilha*. The father-in-law cut poles and collected a bundle of reeds called *Esiiseke*, then took the boy to the place where he would construct the house. No further description of house plans, roofs, decoration or settlement organization is provided.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention the hoe *Eyisuuka* as an item included in the *Omukagha*, and describe goat or sheep skin softened with oil of *Embono* as a material used in arrangements for booking a future bride and carrying a girl child.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document the historical *Omuseye wa maama*, a metallic silver or gold wrist band associated with marriage agreements. They also mention the *Ekitambalha kyo kwamutwe*, a cloth covering the head, in the contemporary form of the marriage gift for the mother-in-law. No tattoos, scarification, henna, hair practices or other forms of body adornment are described.

## Music & performance

They do describe performance in ritual contexts. At the funeral of a circumcised Mukonzo man, a special traditional dance called *Omukumu* was performed as part of the final funeral rites. Only circumcised men were permitted to perform the dance, drum and dance with women.

*Omukumu* also formed part of the *Olhusumba* circumcision ceremony. Women were allowed at the site at the beginning of the ceremony to participate in the traditional dance and on the final day, when the fully healed *Abathende* were brought out of the *Omupinda*. The women who danced the Omukumu were permitted to dismantle the hut.

## Dance & theatre

The named dance in the sources is *Omukumu*. It was connected both with the final funeral rites of a circumcised man and with the beginning and end of the *Olhusumba* circumcision ceremony. During the circumcision ritual, the performance helped mark the entry and departure of the *Abathende*, the candidates undergoing circumcision.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe life-cycle rituals involving birth, circumcision, marriage and death.

Birth names follow the precedence of birth. Boys and girls each have eight principal birth-order names. A first-born boy can be called *Baluku* or *Mutoha*, while a first-born girl is called *Masika*. Other names are associated with twins, the death of an elder child, the survival of grandparents, harvest, changing gender sequence among children and other circumstances. The elder twin is called *Nguru* and the other *Ndobya* regardless of sex. The mother and father of twins are called *Nyabahasa* and *Isebahasa*.

The circumcision ritual *Eribania* was required for a Mukonzo male to be regarded as a man and to marry. Boys were commonly circumcised between the ages of 8 and 18. The annual mass ceremony *Olhusumba* was last held in 1973 according to the source and was later described as being revived. Candidates, called *Abathende* or *Bathende*, were grouped together and made an *Olhuthende*, a march or pilgrimage to the ceremonial venue. Healing lasted one to two months.

The marriage ritual *Erithahya* required the groom to be circumcised, and the sources state that unmarried girls were required to be virgins. The introduction ceremony *Erisunga* brought the groom’s father and uncles to meet the bride’s family and discuss the *Omukagha*, or dowry. The marriage was recognized after the agreed dowry was paid. The sources also describe funeral practices involving *Omukumu*.

## Foodways

The sources describe the Konjo as traditionally agriculturalists and animal husbanders. Crops named include yams, beans, sweet potatoes, peanuts, soy beans, potatoes, rice, wheat, cassava, coffee, bananas, cocoa and cotton. Animals kept include goats, sheep and poultry. They do mention food and drink in marriage contexts. *Ekongotha* is a local brew called Tonto and carried in an *Ekisya*, a large calabash that can accommodate 40 litres or two jerry cans of 20 litres each. During *Erisunga*, the person carrying the brew takes a sip to demonstrate that it is safe, and a representative of the bride’s family tastes it using the same cup. The *Omukagha* includes 12 *Ebisya* of Tonto, or 24 jerry cans of 20 litres each, with alternatives involving crates of soda and beer. A physical goat called *Fumura kigambo* is slaughtered as an ice breaker for the dowry conversation when another animal has not already been slaughtered.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources record two traditions concerning Konjo origins. One legend says that the Bakonzo once lived on Mount Elgon in Eastern Uganda and came with Kintu during the Kintu migrations to Buganda. Rather than settling there, they continued to the western highlands of Mt. Rwenzori, whose climate was said to resemble that of Mount Elgon. This migration is said to have occurred around A.D. 1300.

Another tradition asserts that the Bakonzo have lived on Mount Rwenzori from time immemorial and have no foreign place of origin. According to this account, their ancestor emerged from one of the caves of Mount Rwenxori and produced the rest of the Bakonzo.

## Language & religion

Konjo is described as a Bantu language spoken by the Konjo people. The sources also note that Konjo may refer to the Bantu language of the Ugandan Konjo, while Coastal Konjo and Highland Konjo are Austronesian languages spoken in Sulawesi, Indonesia. No writing system is described in the supplied material.

The Konjo practice traditional religions, Islam and Christianity. According to the 2002 Census of Uganda, 44.1% of Bakonzo were Anglican, 28.7% Roman Catholic, 15.4% Seventh-day Adventist, 6.9% Muslim, 3.1% Pentecostal and 1.5% followed other religions. Ritual accounts refer to sacrifices to gods, including the slaughter of *Embene eye Eyakibanga* in a former pregnancy-related marriage practice and *Embene yo Buwuma* in a marriage between people of the same clan. The source states that the first tradition is no longer practiced, while the second is still practiced.
